I’ll load the project-local instructions first, then inspect the app structure and the smallest files likely responsible for Google Drive video rendering before making a scoped patch.
`rg` is not installed in this container, so I’m falling back to `find`/`sed` for the same narrow inspection.
I found the local policy files and the generated React app files. Next I’m checking those policies plus the generated page components/data where the video embed is most likely defined.
The scoped policy confirms this is a medium, narrow frontend fix and explicitly says not to start runtime servers. I’m now locating the video implementation and any Google Drive URL handling.

The current cards only render static thumbnail images, and the seeded Drive IDs are placeholder-style values, so a Drive-hosted video URL would never be shown as playable media. I’m checking the backend response shape before patching the card renderer.

The backend returns `thumbnailLink` and `webViewLink` for Drive files, while the frontend only tries an image thumbnail. I’m going to add a Drive URL normalizer and render an embeddable preview iframe with a branded fallback when the image path is not enough.

I’m patching only the generated React surface and its companion CSS: the card will accept Drive IDs or shared links, create the `/file/d/.../preview` embed, and keep the existing animated thumbnail fallback for placeholders or missing Drive data.

The renderer now builds a Drive preview URL from either API `webViewLink`, explicit preview fields, thumbnail URLs, or pasted file IDs. I’m tightening the thumbnail styling around the requested Media Studio palette without touching the rest of the app.

The CSS now applies the requested Media Studio colors specifically to the video preview area while keeping text contrast on existing controls. I’m doing static checks only, per the instruction not to run npm/Vite/playground validation.
`git` is not available in this container, so I can’t use `git diff --check`. I’m doing direct source inspection of the patched sections instead.
The sliced inspection cut through JSX mid-block, so I’m checking the complete patched card and running a JSX parse through the project’s installed parser without invoking npm or a server.

There is no parser package visible under `node_modules`, so a real JSX parse/build is not available without running npm. I’m still validating the URL normalization behavior directly with Node, which does not start any app runtime.

Implemented the scoped Google Drive video fix.

I’ll load the project-local policy files first, then inspect the app structure and the smallest set of source files that control connection state, data display, and video playback. After that I’ll patch only the relevant sections and avoid runtime/server commands as requested.

`rg` is not installed in this image, so I’m falling back to `find`/`grep`. The local policy confirms this is a medium scoped frontend edit, with PlutoMix retaining completion authority and no runtime server validation.

The app is a generated Vite React surface with the main behavior concentrated in `src/generated/generatedPage.jsx` and `src/generated/catalogData.js`; the grep hits show mock users/videos and Google Drive iframe previews. I’m reading those plus the backend catalog path before editing so the frontend and API fallback behavior stay aligned.

There are two important implementation issues: the frontend falls back to hardcoded videos/users when the backend is unavailable, and thumbnails currently embed the Google Drive preview iframe directly in each card. I’m going to replace that with empty real-data states, cached Drive connection metadata, and an internal video modal that opens per selected video instead of rendering Drive’s player in every tab/card.

I’m keeping the change narrow: `catalogData.js` will stop shipping fake users/video rows, the backend will stop seeding fake videos and will keep OAuth token expiry in cache, and the generated React page will use configured users, connection cache, empty states, and a SpyDash-owned player route. The brand colors will be applied through CSS variables so existing layout is preserved.

I’m applying the source edits now. The main points are removing shipped preview accounts/video rows, changing data fallbacks to empty real-data states, and adding a `#/player/...` route that opens a SpyDash player in a separate browser tab.

The first pass removed hardcoded users/videos and session defaults. I’m also zeroing the shipped category counts and removing preset folder IDs so the folder map comes only from admin linking or backend Drive sync, not fabricated IDs.

Next I’m changing the React behavior. The card click will write the selected video to local storage and open `#/player/<id>` in a new tab; that route renders SpyDash’s own `<video>` player when a direct media URL is available and otherwise shows a real-data “source not playable” state with the Drive file link.
The player route is now being added around the existing generated route shell. I’m also making admin fallback lists empty rather than falling back to previously bundled video rows.

I found one page-level handoff: `DashboardPage` wasn’t forwarding the new player opener, and the home hero still displayed the old fabricated catalog count. I’m patching those small route files so no stale dummy numbers remain in the visible surface.

I’m aligning the backend fallback with the frontend now. That means no seeded video rows in `/api/catalog`, no fake category counts, and the OAuth access token cache gets expiry metadata so an established connection is reused until it actually expires.
The visual work is next: I’m introducing the requested palette as reusable CSS variables and adding player/empty-state styles without changing the broader layout structure.

I’ll load the project-local policy files first, then inspect the relevant app source around Google Drive/video loading and tab state before making a scoped patch.
`rg` isn’t installed in this environment, so I’m falling back to `find`/`grep` and keeping the search narrow.
The policy files are present. I’m reading those plus a filtered source file listing now so I can target the loading behavior without touching unrelated generated output.

I found the generated React surface under `src/generated`. Next I’m inspecting the route shell, dashboard page, data module, and CSS because the symptom likely sits in the generated dashboard’s Drive/video rendering path.

The app already caches Drive connection state in `localStorage`, but the catalog fetch pulls every folder’s thumbnails in one `Promise.all`, which blocks first render until all folder calls finish. I’m going to change that to show cached/base results immediately, then append folder results as each request returns, while keeping the existing cross-tab connection refresh behavior.

The backend endpoints already support folder-level thumbnail requests, so the narrow frontend fix is enough: keep the initial catalog request, render any returned videos immediately, and stream folder batches into the grid as they arrive.

I’m applying a small patch inside `VideoLibrary`: add a session-backed Drive catalog cache, dedupe incremental videos by Drive/file id, and update the status as folder thumbnail batches arrive instead of waiting for every folder.
I’m editing only `src/generated/generatedPage.jsx` and a small CSS status style so users get immediate results, incremental loading feedback, and shared catalog cache updates between tabs.
The code patch is in place. I’m doing static inspection now, without starting Vite/npm, to catch JSX or control-flow mistakes introduced by the incremental fetch path.

`git` is not available in this shell, so I’m verifying by direct file inspection instead of a diff. I noticed the current patch is functional, but I’m tightening one edge case so aborting a request doesn’t overwrite the visible status.
I’ll make one small follow-up edit to avoid status churn during aborts, then I’ll use an installed parser if available for static JSX validation without running the app.

One existing cross-tab handler could rewrite the connection timestamp on every storage notification. I’m tightening that now so tabs reuse the same Drive connection marker instead of bouncing fresh timestamps between windows.

Implemented the scoped Drive loading fix in [generatedPage.jsx](/workspace/money/apps/spydash/src/generated/generatedPage.jsx:31).

What changed:
- Added per-view Drive catalog caching in `localStorage` so loaded video results can continue across tabs.
- Changed folder thumbnail loading from blocking `Promise.all` to incremental per-folder fetches, so base/cached results render immediately and new videos populate as each folder returns.
- Tightened the Drive connection storage handler so tabs share the same connection marker without repeatedly rewriting timestamps.

instruction:
Replace Google Drive as the primary video playback/storage layer with a production-ready object-storage architecture, while preserving Google Drive as an optional import, export, and backup integration.

Repository objective:
Upgrade the existing vidDb/spydash video dashboard so that videos are stored and served from object storage instead of being streamed directly from Google Drive.

Primary implementation target:
- Google Cloud Storage as primary video storage
- PostgreSQL or the repository’s existing database for video metadata
- Private objects with short-lived signed playback URLs
- Direct resumable uploads from browser to storage
- Thumbnail generation
- Optimized MP4 playback initially
- Architecture ready for future HLS, transcoding, and CDN support
- Google Drive retained only for optional import/export/backup

Mandatory constraints:
1. Do not remove or break any existing feature.
2. Do not delete the existing Google Drive integration.
3. Refactor Google Drive so it is no longer the default video streaming backend.
4. Preserve current authentication, routing, user management, dashboard layout, project structure, and deployment behavior.
5. Inspect the repository before making changes.
6. Reuse existing services, schemas, API conventions, database libraries, UI components, logging, and environment-variable patterns.
7. Do not introduce dummy data.
8. Do not hard-code credentials, bucket names, URLs, ports, users, or tokens.
9. Never expose Google credentials, service-account credentials, access tokens, refresh tokens, or storage signing credentials to the frontend.
10. Implement changes incrementally and keep the application runnable after each major step.
11. Add migrations instead of manually changing production database state.
12. Preserve backward compatibility for existing Google Drive video records.
13. Add clear errors and operational logs without logging secrets.
14. Use strict validation for all user-controlled filenames, IDs, MIME types, and upload metadata.
15. Do not mark the task complete until build, lint, tests, and core flows pass.

Expected architecture:

Browser dashboard
    |
    |-- GET /api/videos
    |       Returns paginated lightweight metadata only
    |
    |-- POST /api/videos/upload-session
    |       Backend authenticates user and creates upload session
    |
    |-- Direct resumable upload
    |       Browser uploads directly to Google Cloud Storage
    |
    |-- POST /api/videos/:id/upload-complete
    |       Backend verifies object and starts processing
    |
    |-- POST /api/videos/:id/playback-session
    |       Backend verifies authorization and returns a short-lived URL
    |
    |-- Object storage
    |       Originals, processed MP4, thumbnails, future HLS files
    |
    |-- Database
            Video metadata, ownership, storage keys, status and audit data

Implement in the following phases.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PHASE 1 — REPOSITORY DISCOVERY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Before editing:

1. Read the root AGENTS.md and all relevant nested instruction files.
2. Inspect:
   - frontend framework and router
   - backend framework
   - current Google Drive implementation
   - current video list and video player
   - authentication middleware
   - database implementation
   - existing upload endpoints
   - Docker configuration
   - environment loading
   - logging
   - tests
3. Identify:
   - where Google OAuth tokens are stored
   - where Drive file IDs are stored
   - how videos are loaded into the dashboard
   - whether playback currently uses Drive URLs or backend proxying
   - whether the backend supports HTTP range requests
4. Produce a concise implementation plan before changing code.
5. List files expected to be modified.
6. Highlight any assumptions.

Do not begin implementation until repository discovery is complete.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PHASE 2 — STORAGE PROVIDER ABSTRACTION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Create a provider-neutral video-storage abstraction.

Suggested interface:

```ts

  createUploadSession(input: CreateUploadSessionInput): Promise<UploadSession>;

    objectKey: string,

  ): Promise<SignedUrlResult>;
  deleteObject(objectKey: string): Promise<void>;
  objectExists(objectKey: string): Promise<boolean>;

I’ll load the project-local policy files first, then inspect the video viewer/player code path and patch only the failing Google Drive thumbnail/playback handling.
`rg` is not installed in this environment, so I’m falling back to `find` and `grep` for the same narrow inspection.
I found the local policy files. Next I’m reading those plus the likely app structure, then I’ll inspect the specific files that define the viewer and player routes.
The project policy is loaded. The app is a generated React/Vite surface with backend video helpers; I’m narrowing now to `src` and `backend/src` video references so the edit stays scoped.

The relevant logic is concentrated in `src/generated/generatedPage.jsx` and `backend/src/server.js`. I’m reading the exact helper and route sections before editing, because the symptoms point to route navigation plus Drive proxy URL handling.

I’ve confirmed the crash risk: the player relies on a localStorage handoff keyed by a URL id, so a direct reload or missed handoff leaves `video` null and can crash when thumbnail/playback helpers read it. I’m checking the surrounding player JSX and Drive mapping before patching the smallest pieces.

The front end already has fallback thumbnail sources, but it can overshoot them indefinitely on image errors and the player cannot reconstruct a Drive video from the URL. I’m going to make the player id stable on the Drive file id, add a safe URL fallback for direct player loads, and cap thumbnail fallback state.
I’m editing only `src/generated/generatedPage.jsx`: stable Drive file-id extraction, cached player recovery, and safer Drive thumbnail/playback sources. No package or runtime files will be touched.
The core recovery helpers are in place. I’m now wiring the player to use them and tightening the image fallback so failed thumbnails do not keep advancing state after the fallback list is exhausted.

The player now reconstructs Drive video context from localStorage catalogs or the Drive id in `#/player/...`, so a direct player tab will not depend on a fragile one-key handoff. I’m running a syntax-only check next; it does not start Vite or any playground runtime.
The grep check shows the intended patch points only. The syntax check is still running, so I’m polling it before I close out.

The syntax-only Node check could not parse `.jsx` files in this project without the build toolchain, and I’m not allowed to run npm/Vite here. I’m doing a final file inspection around the changed sections instead.

- Google Drive player IDs now prefer the real Drive file id instead of `drive-...` wrapper ids.
- Player pages can recover video context from localStorage player cache, cached Drive catalogs, or the Drive id in `#/player/...`, so direct/reloaded player URLs no longer fall into a broken state.
- Drive playback fallback now builds `/api/videos/:fileId/stream` for Drive videos.
- Thumbnail fallback now stops cleanly after available sources are exhausted ins

The project policy is loaded. The task is medium, but the requested fix looks localized: recover gracefully when the PlutoMix API server drops and align the generated UI palette with the supplied brand colors.

I found the failures coming from `src/generated/generatedPage.jsx`: the catalog fetch has no offline fallback, and thumbnails prefer the local proxy first, so a dead backend causes noisy broken images before Drive fallbacks can help.

I’m going to patch the generated source in place: keep cached catalog data visible on fetch failures, prefer direct Drive thumbnail URLs before the local proxy, and update the generated brand palette without changing the app structure.

The CSS already uses the supplied color values as root tokens, so I’ll keep the visual change minimal: rename the ambiguous token names and adjust dependent references, rather than redesigning sections.

I’m checking the local proxy/backend wiring now because the `ERR_CONNECTION_RESET` at `/api/catalog` may be caused by an unhandled backend path, not just the React component. I’ll avoid starting anything per the handoff constraints.

I’ll make two focused fixes: guard the backend catalog endpoint so database or Drive metadata failures return a controlled response instead of taking down the server, and make the generated page resilient when that API is temporarily unavailable.

The backend catalog route now fails closed with a JSON 503 and in-memory catalog fallback instead of allowing an unhandled async failure to reset the connection. Next I’m patching the generated page fallback and thumbnail ordering.

The generated page now keeps cached catalog records visible when `/api/catalog` is unavailable, and thumbnails try the direct Drive image before the local proxy so a dead backend no longer blocks the first thumbnail candidate.
The root brand tokens now carry the provided palette names more accurately. I’m doing a mechanical reference update so the existing design keeps the same accessible contrast behavior.
`perl` is not installed here, so I’ll use an explicit patch for the remaining CSS token references.

The narrow code changes are in place. I’m doing non-runtime validation now: syntax check for the backend file and static inspection of the edited generated sections, without starting npm, Vite, Docker, or health checks.
One refinement: since the backend now returns useful fallback JSON with a 503, the generated page should consume that payload instead of discarding it solely because of the status code.

The frontend now accepts fallback catalog JSON even when the server correctly marks the API as temporarily unavailable, so cached or in-memory videos can still render. I’m reviewing the final diff now.
`node --check` passes for the backend. `git` is not installed in this container, so I can’t show a git diff; I’m using direct file inspection for the edited ranges instead.
